prime.problem: An agent that is fast per call can still take ages to finish, because it makes many calls, re-sends its growing history, hits slow outliers, and sometimes produces a wrong result you have to redo. Timing one call tells you almost nothing about when you'll have something you can trust.
prime.fits: The second map. The first overview explained one model call; this one puts that call in a loop and adds reliability. Its formula divides one attempt's time by the chance the attempt is right, and the agent cards each explain one term.
expect: the top of the fraction (each attempt is slower)
the bottom of the fraction (fewer attempts succeed)
prime.goal: Explain why checking each step is usually the biggest lever for agents, and place every agent card on the fraction.

attend: Why does the formula divide by the success probability instead of adding a retry term?
Which terms in the top of the fraction grow with the number of calls, and which grow faster than the number of calls?
Why can a checked agent that is slower per step reach a correct result sooner than an unchecked fast one?
Which lever touches both the top and the bottom of the fraction?
When is one careful call better than any loop at all?

must: Every step must go right and failures are silent → success = p<sup>N</sup> → falls fast with N → expected attempts = 1 ÷ p<sup>N</sup> → a failed attempt costs the whole task
Checking each step against reality → a bad step costs one retry, not the whole task → the denominator jumps (12.2% → 98.0% for 20 steps at p = 0.9) → checking beats any speed lever
Each call re-sends the history and some calls land in the tail → attempt time grows faster than the call count → cache the stable prefix, parallelise independent steps, budget for p95/p99
Model size moves both sides → a small model makes easy steps faster, but the wrong model for a hard step lowers p → route by step type and escalate on a failed check
elevated: Retries only help when tries are independent → systematic errors fail the same way every time → change something between tries or put a person at irreversible steps
reference: the exact lever table numbers ($2.94 → $0.47, 22.42 s → 12.36 s, 39.5%)
the vocabulary list (throughput, p50/p99, availability, pass^k)
the card-to-term mapping in the diagram

compress.prompt: Close the card and write the time-to-correct-result formula from memory. Draw the four things that stretch an attempt and the one that spoils it, with an arrow from each to the part of the fraction it changes. Finish with the order of the takeaway in one line.
checklist: top: sum over calls of (TTFT + tokens ÷ speed) + tools + retries
context growth and tail latency stretch the top; compounding errors shrink the bottom
checking changes the denominator and is the biggest lever
order: check first, then trim (cache, parallelise, route), then handle the tail

retrieve.q: Explain "time to a correct result" to someone who only measures agent speed in seconds per call. Why is it the number that matters?
answer: an attempt that ends wrong has to be repeated or fixed by you
so expected time = attempt time ÷ chance the attempt is right
it folds speed and reliability into one number you can compare across setups

retrieve.q: Walk through the example: 10 unchecked steps of 2.91 s at p = 0.90. Compute the time to a correct result, then say what testing each step changes and why the result drops to 37.9 s.
answer: with a test per step, a failure retries only that step: 10 × (2.91 + 0.5) ÷ 0.90 = 37.9 s

retrieve.q: You have one afternoon to speed up an agent that often ends with a wrong result. Rank caching the prefix, adding step checks and switching to a faster host, and justify the order.
answer: checks first: they raise the denominator, which dominates when failures are common
caching next: cheap, cuts the growing re-sent history
faster host last: only shrinks the top, and wrong results still repeat

compare.q: The call overview ranks levers by speed-up; this one ranks them by effect on the time to a correct result. Which lever moves most between the two rankings, and what design choice of an agent causes that?
answer: checking isn't on the call overview at all, but tops this one
because an agent chains N steps and a wrong step spoils the task
per-token speed levers drop in relative value once failures dominate

compare.q: Goodput and SLOs judge a server by requests that meet a target; this card judges an agent by correct results per unit time. What is the shared idea, and what does each one count as waste?
answer: shared: raw speed is not the goal; only useful outcomes count
the server counts requests that miss their latency target as waste
the agent counts attempts that end wrong (or time out) as waste

predict.q: Keep 10 steps of 2.91 s but raise per-step success from 0.90 to 0.95, still with no checks. Is the new time to a correct result closer to 83.5 s or to 37.9 s? Commit, then reveal.
predict.answer: 0.95<sup>10</sup> = 0.599, so 29.1 ÷ 0.599 ≈ 48.6 s. A better model helps a lot, but checking the fast model (37.9 s) still wins. With checks, the p = 0.95 model would be 10 × 3.41 ÷ 0.95 ≈ 35.9 s: checks and a better model stack.

apply.task: Take an agent task you ran recently (Claude Code, Cursor or a script). Count or estimate N, the average step time, and whether each step was checked (tests, type check, validator). Fill in the formula for your task, then redesign it: which one step would you add a check to, or split, or run in parallel, to cut the time to a correct result most?
apply.done: You have your task's formula with numbers, one redesign, and a before/after estimate that shows which part of the fraction changed.
apply.hint: If you can't measure p, bracket it: compute the result at p = 0.9 and p = 0.99 and see whether your redesign wins in both.
